source.title: Alignment with human representations supports robust few-shot learning

record.tranche_reason: Tests human-model representational alignment using multiple similarity measures and examines how alignment changes with model scaling; its findings qualify claims of a general scale trend and metric independence.
record.gate_note: The paper measures alignment between vision models and human judgments, not convergence between independently trained models. It reports scaling comparisons for ResNet, ResNet-RS, and Swin Transformer. Few-shot and robustness results are about downstream consequences of human alignment, not model-to-model convergence; the dataset-specific predictive results are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The study measures how well 491 ImageNet vision models align with aggregated human similarity judgments. It then relates that alignment to few-shot learning and robustness. It never measures similarity between independently trained models, across seeds, across modalities, by mapping, or by shared features, so its results do not bear on any version as worded. Model-to-human alignment is a related but different construct (a different party). Representation convergence between models appears only in a related-work citation of Moschella et al. The human-alignment findings belong under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors find that highly human-aligned models few-shot learn better and are more robust to natural adversarial examples and domain shift. The relation with few-shot learning and domain-shift robustness is U-shaped, so alignment is sufficient but not necessary. Alignment's predictive power is domain-specific.
record.recipe_differences: Measures model-to-human alignment using similarity judgments and triplets, then relates it to model scaling and downstream performance; it does not measure convergence between independently trained models.
record.method_sensitivity: Alignment metrics differ in their correlations with each other; predictive effect size for few-shot performance decreases from CIFAR100 to FMNIST and further to MNIST.

fits_no_version.finding: Within architecture families, scaling changes alignment with human similarity judgments inconsistently. ResNet depth and Swin size raise it, while ResNet-RS depth does not. Distillation and ImageNet-21k pre-training raise it; VGG batch-norm and EfficientNet pruning lower it (qualitative).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Model-to-human representational alignment increases with scale and training choices in some but not all vision model families.

fits_no_version.finding: Human-alignment metrics largely agree across 491 models: Spearman pairwise vs triplet ρ=0.992, Pearson pairwise vs triplet ρ=0.824.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Non-metric human-alignment measures agree almost perfectly; metric (Pearson) measures agree less.

fits_no_version.finding: Human alignment has a U-shaped relation with few-shot accuracy. Its predictive effect is strongest on CIFAR100 and weaker on FMNIST and MNIST.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Human-representation alignment predicts few-shot transfer most strongly on data similar to the alignment stimuli.

record.code_released: not stated; the paper says code and full results are in the supplementary information and would be shared publicly after the anonymity period
record.problems: The scaling comparisons are qualitative and limited to a few architecture families. The paper measures alignment to aggregated human judgments rather than agreement between independently trained models. Alignment scores across evaluation domains are not directly reported; the domain-specificity evidence concerns their predictive relationship with few-shot performance.
record.rows_left_out: Few-shot and robustness results in Figures 3 and 4 and Tables 1 and 2 are not catalogued as convergence results because they report downstream performance conditional on human alignment, not model-to-model similarity or alignment scaling.

untested.parts: No model-to-model similarity measured; scale is related only to human alignment, qualitatively, for three families.
No mapping, stitching or relative-representation transfer.
No model-to-model convergence measured under different metrics, settings or inputs.
No test of plateau or of the causes of model-to-model alignment.

record.verdict_notes: Relation changed from tests/T5 to cites_only/T6. The record treated model-to-human alignment as if it were model-to-model convergence. All V1 and V6 links and verdicts are removed, and the results are recorded under fits_no_version. The study's only contact with convergence is a related-work sentence citing Moschella et al. on relative representations converging.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test convergence between independently trained models with different architectures, objectives, data, or modalities; scaling evidence is limited to a few architecture-family comparisons.
No paired image-caption vision-language alignment test.
No comparison of seeds, shared features, or subspaces across same-architecture models.
No mapping, stitching, relative-representation communication, or unpaired alignment test.
No recurring interpretable feature or circuit analysis.
Compares alignment metrics but does not test changes in measured alignment itself across input distributions, metric settings such as neighbour count, or other out-of-distribution stimuli.
Does not test whether model-to-model alignment plateaus or whether shared training data or objectives explain such alignment.

rows.subject: 491-model set
rows.operation_detail: Correlated Spearman pairwise alignment scores with triplet alignment scores across models.
rows.locator: Section 5, “Which alignment metric should we be using?”
rows.note: The measures are very highly correlated, but this does not establish identical alignment estimates.
rows.check: This is the correlation across models between two metrics of human alignment (Spearman pairwise vs triplet, ρ=0.992). It is not model-to-model convergence, so it cannot bear on V6. The 'partial' state is also wrong: ρ=0.992 is near-identity agreement between metrics.

rows.subject: 491-model set
rows.operation_detail: Correlated Pearson pairwise alignment scores with triplet alignment scores across models.
rows.locator: Section 5, “Which alignment metric should we be using?”
rows.note: The authors describe the association as strong but below the Spearman-triplet association.
rows.check: Pearson pairwise vs triplet human-alignment correlation (ρ=0.824). This compares metrics of model-to-human alignment, not of convergence between models, so it is not V6 evidence.

rows.subject: ResNet
rows.operation_detail: Compared models as ResNet depth increased.
rows.note: The authors state that few-shot learning performance does not improve in this comparison.
rows.check: This measures alignment with human judgments, not between models, so it does not bear on V1. It is also a qualitative statement from the Supplement-based architecture insights, with no numbers or specific depths given.

rows.subject: ResNet-RS
rows.operation_detail: Compared models as ResNet-RS depth increased.
rows.note: The authors report increased few-shot learning performance, but not increased alignment.
rows.check: Model-to-human alignment (ResNet-RS depth does not increase it), so it is not V1 evidence. It is qualitative only.

rows.subject: Swin Transformer
rows.operation_detail: Compared Swin Transformer models as size increased.
rows.note: The authors also report that few-shot learning performance increases.
rows.check: Model-to-human alignment (Swin size increases it), so it is not V1 evidence. It is qualitative only.

rows.subject: 491-model set
rows.operation_detail: Related Pearson alignment z² scores to few-shot transfer performance across datasets.
rows.measure: Correlation between human-alignment score and few-shot transfer performance
rows.value: figure only; text says the correlation is statistically significant
rows.locator: Figure 4, right; Section 4.1, “Alignment is a domain-specific metric”
rows.note: The paper reports significant correlations for all three transfer datasets and says the effect is strongest for CIFAR100.
rows.check: Correctly unlinked. This is a downstream predictive correlation (human alignment z² vs few-shot accuracy) and says nothing about convergence.

rows.subject: 491-model set
rows.operation_detail: Related Pearson alignment z² scores to few-shot transfer performance across datasets.
rows.measure: Correlation between human-alignment score and few-shot transfer performance
rows.value: figure only; text says the correlation is statistically significant and its effect size is lower than for CIFAR100
rows.locator: Figure 4, right; Section 4.1, “Alignment is a domain-specific metric”
rows.note: FMNIST is described as more different from the alignment and pre-training datasets than CIFAR100.
rows.check: Correctly unlinked. The correlation is significant but its effect size is smaller than for CIFAR100.

rows.subject: 491-model set
rows.operation_detail: Related Pearson alignment z² scores to few-shot transfer performance across datasets.

rows.note: MNIST is described as completely different from the datasets used to measure alignment.
rows.check: Correctly unlinked. The correlation is significant but its effect size is smallest on MNIST.
